title: Ada and the Kitchen
premise: Quentin Joubert, a part-time novelist who keeps her late grandfather's lighthouse and her heart under strict lock, is stranded by a snowstorm with two men from her past: Elias, the rival novelist she loved at twenty-three, and Theo, the estate lawyer quietly dissolving the inheritance she's been fighting to keep. As the storm traps them in the keeper's cottage, old letters, a contested will, and one unforgettable shared mistake force every buried truth into the light. Quentin learns that loyalty to memory has been her way of hiding, and that the lighthouse—and her heart—must be risked, not merely maintained. She ends the book by choosing to claim both the lighthouse and Elias, signing the deed over to the coastal trust rather than losing either man to silence.
about_author: Noor Okonkwo is a former pastry chef turned novelist who writes love stories set in places where the weather does half the talking. She lives between Lagos and a rented cottage on the Atlantic coast, where she collects lighthouse postcards and unfinished manuscripts.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She catalogs the lighthouse, the failing inheritance case, and her rules for the heart, introducing her discipline of 'training' feeling like a muscle. Emotional beat: controlled loneliness disguised as competence.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A blizzard closes the coast road just as two cars arrive: Elias, her old rival, and Theo, the estate lawyer with papers that could end her tenancy. Beat: dread sharpened into curiosity.

chapters.title: Three at the Table
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Forced dinner in the cottage; old rivalries surface over cold stew and warmer wine. He notices Theo watching Quentin with something more than legal interest. Beat: the past refusing to stay past.

chapters.title: The Best Mistake of Our Twenties
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. A memory chapter: the Lisbon summer, the manuscript she and Elias co-wrote and never finished, the kiss that ended the friendship. Beat: tenderness curdling into old shame.

chapters.title: Papers on the Table
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He reveals the will's fine print: the lighthouse passes to a cousin unless Quentin can prove continuous residence and purpose. He offers a loophole—and an ulterior motive. Beat: the ground shifting under her.

chapters.title: Generators and Ghosts
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. The power fails; the three keep the light burning by hand. Quentin and Elias fall into their old co-writing rhythm against her will. Beat: dangerous, familiar joy.

chapters.title: What Theo Knows
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Alone with the case files, he finds a letter from Quentin's grandfather that changes the inheritance picture—and decides, guiltily, to hold it back. Beat: loyalty beginning to rot.

chapters.title: The Letter in the Wall
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Repairing storm damage, she finds her grandfather's hidden correspondence: he knew about Lisbon, about Elias, about everything. Beat: feeling seen across decades.

chapters.title: Rival by Candlelight
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He confesses he published their shared novel's ending as his own breakthrough, and has hated himself since. Beat: confession as first real intimacy.

chapters.title: The Lawyer's Winter
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Flashback to why he took the case: the cousin who hired him is someone he owes everything to. Beat: sympathy for the antagonist's bind.

chapters.title: Thaw Lines
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She and Elias draft a joint ending to the old novel, laughing, almost touching. Theo watches from the stairs. Beat: the triangle tightening.

chapters.title: The Cousin Arrives Early
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The roads partially clear; the cousin calls with an ultimatum, forcing Theo to choose which truth to tell Quentin. Beat: the clock starting.

chapters.title: Lent Pieces
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She offers Elias a careful, partial reconciliation—friendship, collaboration, nothing more—protecting herself. He accepts too easily. Beat: the cost of half-measures.

chapters.title: The Second Letter
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She finds the rest of her grandfather's letters: he lost the lighthouse once before, to a woman he never told the truth to. Beat: history rhyming, warning.

chapters.title: Betrayal by Briefcase
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She discovers Theo withheld the key letter that could save her claim. Rage, then recognition: he was protecting someone too. Beat: trust inverted.

chapters.title: The Storm's Second Act
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. A worse front hits; the light fails and a fishing boat is in trouble. The three work the mechanism together, rivals and lawyer as one crew. Beat: crisis forging honesty.

chapters.title: Truth at the Top of the Tower
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. In the lantern room, soaked and shaking, she demands full truth from both men—Elias's love, Theo's debt—and gives her own: she was never loyal to memory, just afraid. Beat: the emotional climax.

chapters.title: What the Heart Is For
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. He withdraws his claim to the shared novel, publicly and in writing, freeing her to claim it—and him. Beat: sacrifice as proof.

chapters.title: Theo's Signature
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. He turns over the hidden letter and negotiates a trust arrangement that saves the lighthouse without the cousin. Beat: redemption through honesty.

chapters.title: Deed and Devotion
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. She signs the lighthouse to the coastal trust, keeping the cottage and the light, and asks Elias to stay—not as a rival or a memory, but wholly. Beat: the risked heart answered.

chapters.title: Spring Tide
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Weeks later: the novel published under both names, the light automated but tended, Theo a friend and occasional visitor. Beat: quiet joy, earned.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Daughter
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, closing frame. She finishes the book we've been reading, dedicating it to the grandfather who taught her that a light is kept, not owned. Beat: memory and truth finally reconciled.
